newsitem.title: UK: Rainbow dreamers float past UK parliament.
newsitem.headline: Rainbow dreamers float past UK parliament.

text.p: The political party which wants to get rid of all politicians took their message to the heart of government on a late-night cruise past Britain's parliament.

"People call us dreamers, in fact I call myself an apprentice prophet. But I believe our time is coming," said George Weiss, an avuncular, bearded figure who is the founder of the Rainbow Dream Ticket Party.
Rainbow George, as he prefers to be called, stood at the bow of a river launch filled with his supporters, an odd mixture of punks, New Age lifestylers, scientists and musicians.
To ensure levity in the political debate, a clown and a unicyclist were on board.

As the boat passed parliament, a mandolin player serenaded Big Ben with an anthem of the Rainbow suppoters. "We are the Pixie People," rang the chorus from the boat, with accompaniment from aboriginal pipes and bongo drums.

A few spectators on the river terrace beneath Big Ben looked on bemused, perhaps secure in the knowledge that this was the closest the Rainbow Dream Ticket Party would get to entering parliament at the May 1 election.

The Rainbows are a happy bunch, but Rainbow George has a serious message. He believes the days of centralised parliament are over. He maintains that every single person should be empowered to vote on any subject they wish.

"There is no need to pay people to represent us in parliament. We are all capable of making our own decisions. Everybody knows they can make a better job of it than the professional politicians," he said.
"We may get nowhere this time, but I firmly believe that our time will come in about 10 years."

The Rainbow party has more than 30 candidates standing for the May 1 election, but George cheerfully admits the party is likely to lose every deposit of 500 pounds ($800) which aspiring candidates must lodge to prove their commitment.
Candidates get the money back only if they can win five percent of the votes cast in their constituency.
Rainbow George's manifesto spells out the system of "preferendum", by which the public could make their choice on any number of issues.

"In the near future, home-based electronic voting will give us the ability to directly influence all local and national decisions which affect our lives," states Ronnie Carroll, the Rainbow candidate for the London district of Hampstead and Highgate.
Carroll, who gained fame as a singer in the 1960s, is making an appeal which he calculates will reach directly to the voters of his affluent constituency.
"Save the Coffee Cup, Vote Rainbow," his election pamphlet states, referring to a campaign to keep open a well-known cafe.

The Rainbows use music extensively to get their ideas across -- not surprising since most supporters seem to dabble in the music business -- and their manifesto is summed up in the song "Rainbowland", reprinted in the party leaflets.

"In Rainbowland there will be neither need nor greed/Or any use for silly money/No politicians, no preachers, no incompetent teachers/No ignorant views, no business to lose/Nor corrupt instituions or harmful pollutions," the party members sang.
